## Objectives {#objectives}

By the end of this session you can:

- Write and call your own functions.
- Run a function over a list of files with `lapply()`.
- Say how research code differs from software, and which software
  engineering practices are worth borrowing anyway.
- Structure a script so a stranger can read it: sections, names,
  comments that say why.
- Avoid duplicated code and unexplained constants.
- Write code that is easy to check — and explain why that is a
  property of the code, not of the checker.
- Localize a defect by bisection, and pick the right tool for the
  kind of failure you have.
- Document a diagnosis: the line, the mechanism, the fix, and the
  proof.

## What we cover {#coverage}

- Writing functions; `for` loops at reading depth.
- `lapply()` and `sapply()` for real: apply a function to every
  element of a list — every file in a folder, every group in a
  split — the pattern most of the applied work runs on. Lists are
  what they eat and what they return.
- **Research code is not software.** Software has users, ships, and
  is maintained for years; a research script has one author, runs a
  handful of times, and has to produce a number someone can defend.
  So the engineering practices divide in three: the ones that pay off
  immediately here (naming, structure, no duplication, version
  control, small tested pieces), the ones that pay off selectively
  (unit tests, code review, refactoring), and the ones that are
  overhead at this scale (APIs, design patterns, coverage targets,
  CI). Borrow deliberately rather than by reputation.
- Coding practices: naming things, `# section ----` structure,
  comments that explain why rather than what, named constants instead
  of magic numbers, not repeating yourself — you are writing code
  for others, and that includes yourself in six months.
- **Write code that is easy to check.** Checkability is a property of
  how the code is built, not of how hard you look at it afterwards:
  small pieces with one job, intermediate values you can print,
  no step that changes three things at once, and results that come
  out where an assertion can reach them. Code you cannot check is
  code you cannot defend, whatever it computed.
- Test small before you run big; re-run the whole script, not just
  the piece you changed.
- A personal style sheet: eleven dimensions of how *you* write code —
  kept, and paid off later in the semester.
- **Debugging as a strategy, not a toolbox.** Read the error before
  you change anything; reproduce it on the smallest input that still
  fails; form one hypothesis at a time and test it; change one thing
  per run. Then the tools, matched to the failure: `traceback()` for
  where it died, `browser()` for what the state was, print debugging
  for how a value evolved, and bisection for a wrong number that
  never errored at all.
- Bisection — comment out half, re-run, repeat until the defect has
  nowhere to hide. It is the only one of the four that works when
  nothing crashed.
- The in-class bug hunt: a short script that runs clean and reports a
  plausible wrong number. Find it — no AI, in the room.

**Verification habit.** Bisection: where could the wrong number have
entered?
